In 1984, installation of Unit No. 4 would be completed and Units Nos. 3 and 4 would commence commercial operation.
Since the tunnels and powerhouse would be underground, construction could continue year-around, even during inclement weather. During construction, the natural runoff from Bad Creek would be diverted through a steel pipe embedded in concrete in a trench under the main dam.
The project construction would extend over 9 years. The work force during the peak would be approximately 500 persons, and 25 percent of these persons would be transferees from the Applicant's other projects. During the fifth year of construction, the total work force would begin to decline.
1.6 OPERATIONAL AND MAINTENANCE PROCEDURES
Jocassee Reservoir, the proposed lower reservoir, was designed and constructed to provide 41,000 acre-feet of storage between reservoir elevations of 1,086 and 1,080 feet for future pumped storage development. The Bad Creek Project would utilize 30,200 acre-feet of this amount.
The Jocassee Reservoir total storage capacity is 1,143,000 acre-feet, of which 214,000 acre-feet is usable storage with 30-foot maximum drawdown from elevation 1,110. The first 24 feet of drawdown (173,000 acre-feet) is allocated to Jocassee; the remaining 6 feet of drawdown (41,000 acre-feet) is reserved for future pumped storage development.
The Keowee Reservoir, with a gross storage capacity of 911,000 acre-feet, functions as the lower reservoir for Jocassee pumped storage operation. Of the 388,000 acre-feet of usable storage in 25 feet of drawdown, 40,000 acre-feet at 3-foot drawdown is allocated to Jocassee pumped storage. The Keowee development is a conventional hydroplant with an installed capacity of 140 MW.
The Bad Creek upper reservoir would contain 30,228 acre-feet of usable storage between reservoir elevations of 2,310 and 2,150 feet (Figure 1-11). Since the upper reservoir drainage basin is only 1.5 square miles, no significant secondary purposes, such as conservation or flood control, would accrue to the project; however, some benefit would accrue to Jocassee Reservoir, since operating the powerplants in tandem would reduce fluctuations in Lake Jocassee.
